content:
When a flood, cyclone, landslide, fire or other disaster strikes, an Indian NGO that responds usually has hours, not weeks, to put an appeal online. The NGOs that raise money well in those first days are almost always the ones that prepared before the emergency: a ready-made appeal page template, donation forms that already work, pre-approved wording on how funds will be used, and a plan for updates. NGO website development in India should therefore treat an emergency appeal page as a standard part of the site, built and tested in calm times and switched on in minutes when needed. This guide explains what such a page needs, how to word it so donors trust it and your accounts stay clean, how to handle receipts and foreign donations, and how to keep the site up when the appeal spreads on WhatsApp.

It is written for founders, programme heads, fundraising and communications staff at Indian NGOs, trusts and Section 8 companies that respond, or may respond, to emergencies, including those whose usual work is not disaster relief but who help when their own communities are affected.

## Why emergency appeals need preparation, not improvisation

In an emergency, three things happen at once. Staff are busy with the response itself. Donor attention peaks in the first days and then falls quickly as news moves on. And the people who want to give are often strangers who arrived through a forwarded WhatsApp message, a news story or a social post, and who have never heard of your organisation.

Those strangers decide in seconds whether to trust you. An appeal that is just a bank account number in an image, or a donation page with a generic "Support our work" headline, loses them. A clear, specific, credible page wins them. Preparing it in advance means the person writing the appeal during the crisis only has to fill in facts, not design a page and argue about wording.

## What an emergency appeal page must contain

### A clear, factual headline and summary

Lead with what happened, where, and what you are doing. For example: "Floods in [district]: we are distributing food, drinking water and hygiene kits to affected families in [blocks]." Avoid exaggeration. Use figures only from official sources or your own field teams, attributed and dated: "According to the district administration on [date], ..." or "Our team has reached [number] families as of [date]." If you do not yet know, say so.

### Your connection to the affected area

Donors want to know why your organisation is in a position to help. Say how long you have worked in the area, which local partners you work with, and what you have done before. If you are new to the area, be honest about partnering with organisations already there.

### What the money will buy

Specific, costed examples help donors choose an amount and believe the appeal. For example:

- "₹[amount] provides a family food kit for about [number] days."
- "₹[amount] provides a hygiene kit: soap, sanitary pads, buckets, water purification tablets."
- "₹[amount] supports temporary shelter material for one family."

Build these from your actual procurement costs and say they are approximate. Do not borrow numbers from another organisation's appeal. If costs are still being worked out, show the items without amounts and add amounts as soon as you have quotes.

### A donation form that works on the first try

The donation form should be on the same page, near the top on mobile, and should:

- Offer suggested amounts tied to the examples above, plus "other amount".
- Collect only what you need: name, email, mobile, and PAN plus address only if the donor wants an 80G certificate.
- Support UPI, cards and net banking through your existing payment gateway.
- Default to a one-time gift. Monthly giving can be offered afterwards, not pushed during an emergency.
- Show a clear confirmation page and send an email or WhatsApp receipt immediately.

Test the whole flow every quarter, not on the day of the disaster. Our guide to [donation page design](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donation-page-design-2026) covers form details in depth.

### How funds will be used, in honest wording

This is the most important paragraph on the page, and the one most often written in haste. If you say "100% of your donation goes to flood victims in [district]", you have made a promise. If you raise more than you can usefully spend there, or if part of the cost of delivery is administration, you have a problem.

Wording used by many careful NGOs follows this pattern:

> "Donations to this appeal will be used for our relief and recovery work for communities affected by the [event] in [region]. If we raise more than we can responsibly spend on this response, we will use the remainder for our disaster preparedness and recovery work in similar communities, and we will report on how funds were used."

Agree this wording with your trustees and auditor in advance. It keeps you honest with donors and gives your accounts team a clear rule for "restricted" funds. Publish what proportion, if any, goes towards delivery costs such as transport and staff time.

### Updates, dated

Add a dated updates section near the top: "Update, [date]: Our teams reached [number] families in [block] today." Even short updates show donors that the response is real and that you are accountable. Plan who will write them and how often (daily for the first week, then weekly).

### Contact and verification details

Show your registered name, registration details (trust, society or Section 8 company), 12A and 80G status, office address, phone and email. If a journalist or donor wants to check you, everything should be one tap away. Link to your transparency and impact reporting pages and annual reports.

## Tax receipts and foreign donations

Get these right, because emergency donors include many first-time givers who will contact you later about their certificates.

### 80G receipts and donation certificates

If your organisation holds approval for tax-deductible donations (still widely called "80G" approval), eligible donors can claim a deduction. Since 2021 an approved organisation has had to file an annual statement of donations and then issue each donor a donation certificate generated from that statement: Forms 10BD and 10BE under the Income Tax Act, 1961. The Income Tax Act, 2025, which took effect on 1 April 2026, renumbered these as Form 113 (the statement) and Form 114 (the certificate), according to the Income Tax Department's form mapping guide. The statement has been due by 31 May after the end of the financial year, and late filing attracts a penalty. Either way, the instant receipt you send at the time of donation is an acknowledgement; the formal certificate comes later. Say so on the page and in the receipt, so donors are not confused.

Also note that cash donations above ₹2,000 have not been eligible for the deduction, so encourage digital payments. Collect PAN only from donors who want the certificate, and protect it. Our article on 80G compliant donation platforms explains the receipt flow.

This is general information, not tax advice; confirm details with your chartered accountant.

### Foreign contributions

Emergencies attract offers of help from abroad. Under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, an organisation may accept foreign contribution only if it holds FCRA registration or prior permission, and since the 2020 amendment foreign contributions must be received in the designated FCRA account at the State Bank of India, New Delhi Main Branch. If your organisation is not FCRA-registered, your appeal page and payment setup must not accept foreign contributions, and your form should ask donors to confirm they are Indian citizens donating from Indian sources. Our article on the [FCRA amendment rules](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-fcra-amendment-rules-2026) and the FCRA payment gateway setup explain what to configure. When in doubt, ask your CA before you share the appeal internationally.

## Offline and in-kind help

Many people will want to give things, not money: clothes, food, blankets, medicines. Unrequested goods often create sorting and storage problems for relief teams. Add a short section that says clearly:

- Which items you need, if any, and which you cannot accept (for example, used clothing or medicines without proper storage).
- Where and when items can be dropped off, and who to contact first.
- That cash donations are usually the most useful because they let teams buy exactly what is needed locally.

Bank transfers and cheques also arrive in emergencies. Publish your account details as text (not only as an image), state the exact account name, and ask donors to send their details by email or form so you can issue receipts. Our guide to offline donations through bank transfer, cheque and pledges covers how to record them.

Be alert to fraud. Fake appeals using a real NGO's name and photos appear during most major disasters. Tell donors on the page that you only accept donations through this page and the account named on it, and give a phone number to verify.

## Keeping the site up when the appeal goes viral

An appeal shared widely on WhatsApp can send more visitors in an hour than your site normally gets in a month. Shared hosting plans that work fine on ordinary days can slow down or suspend the site exactly when it matters most.

Before any emergency:

- Put the site behind a CDN and cache the appeal page as a static page. Donation forms and payment pages should be separate from the cached page.
- Confirm your payment gateway's limits and contact details so you can raise any limits quickly.
- Load-test the appeal template and donation flow once a year.
- Have a lightweight fallback: a simple static page with the appeal text and donation link that can be served if the main site struggles.

Our guide to [donation site traffic spikes, hosting and load testing](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donation-site-traffic-spikes-hosting-load-testing-2026) explains each step.

### Sharing previews

Most people will see your appeal first as a WhatsApp or social media preview. Set a specific Open Graph title, description and image for the appeal page, so the preview says "Flood relief in [district]" with a real photo rather than your generic homepage banner. Our article on WhatsApp share previews and Open Graph shows how.

## Photographs and dignity

Emergency appeals are tempting places for distressing images. Use photographs that show people with dignity, taken with consent, and avoid identifying children or vulnerable people in ways that could put them at risk. Do not use photos from other disasters or stock libraries presented as your response. Caption each photograph with place and date. The Core Humanitarian Standard, a widely used set of commitments for humanitarian organisations, emphasises accountability to affected people, and that includes how they are represented.

## How to build the template in advance

A practical setup that works on WordPress or a custom site:

1. **An "Emergency appeal" page template** with fixed blocks: headline, summary, your connection, what money buys, donation form, use-of-funds statement, updates, in-kind section, verification details and FAQs.
2. **A dedicated donation campaign** in your donation system, so all appeal gifts are tagged and reportable separately from general donations.
3. **Pre-approved wording** for the use-of-funds statement and receipt messages, signed off by trustees and your CA.
4. **A homepage banner slot** that can be switched on to point to the active appeal.
5. **Receipt and thank-you templates** for email and WhatsApp mentioning the appeal by name.
6. **A tracking setup:** UTM-tagged links for each channel (WhatsApp, Instagram, email, partners) so you know where donations come from. Our guide to donation analytics in GA4 covers this.
7. **A closing procedure:** when the appeal ends, replace the form with a "This appeal has closed" message and a link to general donations, and keep the page live with the final report.

With the template ready, launching an appeal should take an hour or two: write the facts, set costs, add photos, publish, and share.

## After the appeal: reporting back

Donors who give in emergencies often never hear from the organisation again, which is a missed opportunity and, for many, a reason not to give again. Plan a final report on the same page within a few months:

- How much was raised and how it was spent, by category.
- What was delivered and to how many people, with dated figures from your records.
- What remains to be done, and how any surplus is being used under your published statement.
- Thanks to donors and partners.

Email the report to everyone who gave. Some will become long-term supporters.

## What it costs

Indicative ranges for an Indian NGO (not a quote):

- **Appeal template and campaign setup** on an existing WordPress donation site: roughly ₹15,000 to ₹50,000.
- **Hosting hardening, CDN and a load test:** roughly ₹10,000 to ₹40,000, plus any hosting upgrade.
- **A full donation website** with campaign management, receipts and reporting, if you do not have one: see our [NGO website pricing](/pricing/ngo-website).

## Frequently asked questions

### How quickly can an NGO launch an emergency appeal online?

If a template, donation campaign and pre-approved wording are ready, an appeal page can go live within one or two hours of the decision to respond. Without preparation it often takes several days, by which time much donor attention has passed.

### What should an NGO disaster appeal page include?

A factual summary of what happened and what you are doing, your connection to the area, costed examples of what donations buy, a working donation form, a clear statement of how funds will be used including any surplus, dated updates, in-kind guidance and your registration and contact details.

### Can donors get 80G receipts for disaster relief donations?

If your organisation holds 80G approval, eligible donors can claim a deduction. The instant receipt is an acknowledgement; the formal donation certificate (Form 10BE, renumbered Form 114 under the Income Tax Act, 2025) is issued after you file the annual statement of donations, which has been due by 31 May. Cash donations above ₹2,000 have not qualified.

### Can an NGO accept foreign donations for disaster relief?

Only if it holds FCRA registration or prior permission, and foreign contributions must be received in the designated FCRA account at SBI, New Delhi Main Branch. Organisations without FCRA approval must not accept foreign contributions and should ask donors to confirm they are giving from Indian sources.

### What if we raise more money than we need for an emergency?

Say in advance on the appeal page how surplus funds will be used, for example for recovery or disaster preparedness work in similar communities, and report on it. Agree this wording with your trustees and auditor before any emergency.
